questions.prompt: In a Nash equilibrium, what is true of each player's strategy?

options.text: It is a best response to the other players' strategies.
It maximises the sum of all players' payoffs.
It guarantees the player's highest possible payoff.

questions.why: In a Nash equilibrium no player gains by changing strategy alone. Each strategy is a best response to the others.
questions.whyShort: In a Nash equilibrium no player gains by changing strategy alone.

optionWhy.b: That describes a social optimum. An equilibrium only rules out profitable solo deviations.
optionWhy.c: Equilibrium strategies need not be dominant; they only need to be best responses to each other.
optionWhy.d: An equilibrium can leave every player worse off than some other outcome.

questions.prompt: Which outcome is the Nash equilibrium of the one-shot prisoner's dilemma?

options.text: One player cooperates and the other defects

questions.why: Defecting pays more whatever the other player does. So both defect, even though both prefer mutual cooperation.
questions.whyShort: Defecting pays more whatever the other player does.

optionWhy.b: Either player gains by switching to defect, so it is not stable.
optionWhy.c: The cooperating player gains by switching to defect.

questions.prompt: What makes a strategy strictly dominant?

options.text: It pays strictly more than every other strategy, whatever the others do.
It pays more than the other strategies against the most likely opponent move.
It is the strategy most players choose.

questions.why: A strictly dominant strategy beats every alternative against every possible profile of the other players.
questions.whyShort: A strictly dominant strategy beats every alternative against every possible profile of the other players.

optionWhy.b: Dominance must hold against every possible choice of the others.
optionWhy.c: How popular a strategy is has nothing to do with dominance.

questions.prompt: When is an outcome Pareto optimal?

options.text: No other outcome makes someone better off without making someone worse off.
Every player plays a best response.

questions.why: Pareto optimality means no improvement is possible for anyone without a loss for someone else.
questions.whyShort: Pareto optimality means no improvement is possible for anyone without a loss for someone else.

optionWhy.b: A Pareto optimal outcome need not maximise the sum of payoffs.
optionWhy.c: That is the definition of a Nash equilibrium.

questions.prompt: What does a mixed strategy assign?

options.text: A probability to each pure strategy
A different player to each move

questions.why: A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over a player's pure strategies.
questions.whyShort: A mixed strategy is a probability distribution over a player's pure strategies.

optionWhy.b: Payoffs come from the game itself, not from a strategy.
optionWhy.c: A strategy belongs to a single player.

questions.prompt: In a zero-sum game, what holds for every outcome?

options.text: The players' payoffs add up to zero.
Every player gets a payoff of zero.
No player can gain by deviating.

questions.why: In a zero-sum game one player's gain is exactly the other's loss, so payoffs always sum to zero.
questions.whyShort: In a zero-sum game one player's gain is exactly the other's loss, so payoffs always sum to zero.

optionWhy.b: Payoffs can be non-zero as long as they cancel out.
optionWhy.c: That describes an equilibrium, not a zero-sum game.

questions.prompt: Which strategy starts by cooperating and then copies the opponent's previous move?
questions.why: Tit-for-tat opens with cooperation and then mirrors whatever the opponent did in the previous round.
questions.whyShort: Tit-for-tat opens with cooperation and then mirrors whatever the opponent did in the previous round.

optionWhy.b: Grim trigger defects forever after a single defection.
optionWhy.c: Always defect never cooperates.

questions.prompt: What does the folk theorem say about infinitely repeated games?

options.text: Many payoff profiles can be sustained as equilibria when players are patient enough.
Defection in every round is the only equilibrium.
Cooperation is always the unique equilibrium.

questions.why: With enough patience, the threat of future punishment can sustain many outcomes, cooperation included, as equilibria.
questions.whyShort: With enough patience, the threat of future punishment can sustain many outcomes, cooperation included, as equilibria.

optionWhy.b: That holds for a finitely repeated prisoner's dilemma with a known last round.
optionWhy.c: Many equilibria exist, including permanent defection.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the one-shot prisoner's dilemma are true?

options.text: Mutual cooperation is better for both than mutual defection.
Mutual cooperation is a Nash equilibrium.

questions.why: Defection dominates, so the equilibrium is mutual defection, yet both players would prefer mutual cooperation.
questions.whyShort: Defection dominates, so the equilibrium is mutual defection, yet both players would prefer mutual cooperation.

optionWhy.c: Either player gains by switching to defect.
optionWhy.d: Defecting pays more whatever the other player does.

questions.prompt: Which are part of a normal-form game?

options.text: A set of actions for each player
A payoff for each player at each action profile
A fixed order in which the players move

questions.why: A normal-form game lists the players, their actions and the payoffs for every combination of actions.
questions.whyShort: A normal-form game lists the players, their actions and the payoffs for every combination of actions.

optionWhy.d: The normal form models simultaneous choices; move order belongs to the extensive form.

questions.statement: Every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.
questions.why: Nash proved that every finite game has an equilibrium once mixed strategies are allowed.
questions.whyShort: Nash proved that every finite game has an equilibrium once mixed strategies are allowed.

questions.statement: A Nash equilibrium always maximises the sum of the players' payoffs.
questions.why: The prisoner's dilemma equilibrium gives both players less than mutual cooperation would.
questions.whyShort: The prisoner's dilemma equilibrium gives both players less than mutual cooperation would.

questions.statement: If every player has a strictly dominant strategy, playing them is a Nash equilibrium.
questions.why: A strictly dominant strategy is a best response to everything, so nobody gains by deviating.

questions.statement: Tit-for-tat defects in the first round.

questions.prompt: A strategy that pays at least as much as every alternative, whatever the others do, is ___ strategy.
questions.why: Weak dominance means never worse than any alternative, against every choice of the others.
questions.whyShort: Weak dominance means never worse than any alternative, against every choice of the others.

optionWhy.b: A mixed strategy randomises over pure strategies; it says nothing about dominance.
optionWhy.c: Minimax limits the worst case; it need not do as well as every alternative.

questions.prompt: A profile where no player gains by changing strategy alone is ___.
questions.why: That is the definition of a Nash equilibrium: no profitable unilateral deviation.
questions.whyShort: That is the definition of a Nash equilibrium: no profitable unilateral deviation.

optionWhy.b: Pareto optimality compares outcomes, not unilateral deviations.
optionWhy.c: A social optimum maximises the total payoff.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies in order.

options.text: Find a strictly dominated strategy for some player.
Check the smaller game for newly dominated strategies.
Stop when no strictly dominated strategy is left.

questions.why: Removing one dominated strategy can make others dominated, so the check repeats until nothing changes.
questions.whyShort: Removing one dominated strategy can make others dominated, so the check repeats until nothing changes.

questions.why: Tit-for-tat and grim trigger both start nice and only punish defection. Always defect never cooperates.

questions.prompt: What does a rational agent choose?

options.text: The action that maximises its expected performance measure
The action that always turns out best
The action a human expert would take

questions.why: A rational agent picks the action with the best expected performance, given what it has perceived so far.
questions.whyShort: A rational agent picks the action with the best expected performance, given what it has perceived so far.

optionWhy.b: Rationality maximises the expected outcome; it cannot guarantee the actual one.
optionWhy.c: Rationality is judged by the performance measure, not by imitation.

questions.prompt: Which property means the agent's sensors give it the complete state of the environment at each point?
questions.why: In a fully observable environment the sensors capture everything relevant to choosing an action.
questions.whyShort: In a fully observable environment the sensors capture everything relevant to choosing an action.

optionWhy.b: Deterministic is about whether actions have a single predictable result.
optionWhy.c: Static means the world does not change while the agent deliberates.

questions.prompt: In a ReAct loop, what follows each action?

options.text: An observation of the action's result
A new message from the user
A gradient update of the model

questions.why: ReAct alternates thought, action and observation, so each action's result feeds the next thought.
questions.whyShort: ReAct alternates thought, action and observation, so each action's result feeds the next thought.

optionWhy.b: The loop continues without the user until the task is done.
optionWhy.c: ReAct works by prompting; nothing is trained.

questions.prompt: What is bounded rationality?

options.text: Making good decisions within limits of time, information and computation
Refusing to act without complete information
Acting at random when a problem is hard

questions.why: Real agents have limited time and computation, so they settle for decisions that are good enough within those limits.
questions.whyShort: Real agents have limited time and computation, so they settle for decisions that are good enough within those limits.

optionWhy.b: A bounded agent still acts under uncertainty.
optionWhy.c: Bounded rationality still aims for good choices.

questions.prompt: Which step types appear in a ReAct trace?
questions.why: A ReAct trace interleaves thoughts, actions and the observations those actions return.
questions.whyShort: A ReAct trace interleaves thoughts, actions and the observations those actions return.

optionWhy.d: ReAct traces have no reward signal; the model is prompted, not trained.

questions.prompt: Which problems come from several agents learning at the same time?

options.text: The environment looks non-stationary to each agent.
Credit for a shared reward is hard to assign.
Every agent must have a different reward function.
Agents can no longer observe anything.

questions.why: Other learners keep changing their behaviour, and a shared reward does not say which agent earned it.
questions.whyShort: Other learners keep changing their behaviour, and a shared reward does not say which agent earned it.

optionWhy.c: Agents can share a single reward, as in cooperative tasks.
optionWhy.d: Agents still observe the environment, often partially.

questions.statement: In centralised training with decentralised execution, agents need the central information when they act.
questions.why: The central information is used only during training. At execution time each agent acts on its own observations.
questions.whyShort: The central information is used only during training.

questions.why: Each move leads to exactly one next position, with no chance involved.
